An 18-year-old male patient with severe nodulocystic
acne unresponsive to topical remedies and systemic antibio-
tics was given oral isotretinoin (1 mg/kg/day) by a practi-
cing dermatologist subsequent to unremarkable routine
laboratory investigations. Ten days later, he was admitted
to the Department of Dermatology at the Patras University
Hospital complaining of aching and stiffness of his
shoulders, neck, back and thighs. There was no family
history of neuromuscular disease or history of systemic
illness, vigorous physical activity or concomitant intake of
other drugs. Neurological examination showed normal
mental status and cranial nerves. On the up-right position,
the neck was slightly ﬂexed and drawn down into the
shoulder girdle, the arms ﬂexed 308at the elbow, the lumbar
curve exaggerated (hyperlordosis) and the hips as well as
knees ﬂexed 30 8. The patient’s volitional activity was
signiﬁcantly reduced and he moved with great difﬁculty,
like a ‘wooden soldier’ or a ‘robot’. There was marked,
stable resistance to passive movements throughout the
entire range of motion of the neck, shoulders, elbows, hips
and knees. The muscle strength and sensory perception were
normal, the tendon reﬂexes were brisk bilaterally and the
plantar responses ﬂexor. Over the next 2 days the muscle
stiffness continued to worsen and was punctuated by painful
spasms elicited by various startling stimuli such as a touch
on the shoulder or the telephone ringing. The patient was
unable to get out of the bed and walk unaided.
Haemogram and standard blood chemistry were normal.
Particularly, the serum levels (reference range in brackets)
of calcium and phosphorus levels were 9.9 mg/dl (8.3–10.2)
and 4.3 mg/dl (2.7–4.5), respectively, magnesium
2.1 mequiv/l (1.3–2.1), creatine kinase 61 U/l (38–174),
vitamin B
12 425 pg/ml (180–710) and folic acid 2.9 ng/ml
(. 1.5). Endocrine proﬁle showed a serum growth hormone
level 1.5 ng/ml ( , 2), T 4 total 9.9 mg/dl (4.5–12.5), TSH
3.2 mlU/ml (0.4–4.2) and morning serum cortisol level

20 mg/dl (5–23). CSF analysis disclosed two lymphocytes
per mm
3 (up to ﬁve cells), protein 25 mg/dl (15–50) and no
oligoclonal bands. Glucose tolerance value at 120 min was
90 mg/dl (70–120). Total serum protein was 8.2 g/dl (6.0–
8.4) with albumin being 4.9 g/dl (3.5–5.5) and globulin
3.3 g/dl (2.5–3.4). Autoimmune markers, including antinuc-
lear, antistriated muscle, thyroid microsomal, antiphospho-
lipid antibodies and rheumatoid factor were negative (non-
detectable). Assessment of antibodies to glutamic acid
decarboxylase (GAD), the rate-limiting enzyme for the
synthesis of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), and
amphiphysin in the serum or the spinal ﬂuid was not
performed. Brain and chest computerized tomographies,

hands’ X-rays and abdomen ultrasound were unremarkable.
Motor and sensory nerve conduction studies revealed no
abnormalities. Needle electromyography disclosed persis-
tent activation of normal motor units during attempted
relaxation concurrently in agonist and antagonist muscle
pairs, which temporally subsided after an intravenous injec-
tion of 10 mg diazepam (Fig. 1).
Oral isotretinoin was discontinued upon admission of the
patient, who was switched to topical forms of therapy.
Muscle stiffness demonstrated a progressive reduction
over the next few days without any symptomatic treatment
(i.e. muscle relaxants) and completely resolved 2 weeks
after withdrawal of isotretinoin. The patient has presently
completed a 5-year follow-up and reveals no recurrence of
his neurological condition either in clinical or in electrophy-
siological terms.
2. Discussion
SPS is a rare and disabling disorder of unknown etiology
which is characterized by muscle rigidity and episodic
spasms involving the axial and limb musculature [3]. The
occurrence of antibodies against GAD in 60 –70% of
patients, the association of SPS with autoimmune disorders
and other autoantibodies and its response to immunothera-
pies support the autoimmune pathogenesis of this syndrome
[3,4]. Since GABA is the major inhibitory neurotransmitter
in the brain and almost one-third of all synapses are GABA-
ergic, a decrease in GABA concentrations induced by the
anti-GAD antibodies could explain the muscular hyperac-
tivity observed in SPS [3]. Interestingly, several SPS cases
associated with malignancies have also been described [5].
The neurological picture of our patient reveals the typical
features of the SPS: axial and proximal limb muscle stiff-
ness, superimposed painful cramps, lumbar hyperlordosis
and continuous ﬁring of normal motor unit potentials that
was suppressed by diazepam on electromyography [4].
Primary muscle disease as the cause of stiffness could be
ruled out in our patient since there was no clinical or neuro-
physiological evidence of muscle weakness and his serum
CPK levels were normal. Moreover, considering the prox-
imal distribution of symptoms in our patient, his brisk
tendon reﬂexes, the intact sensation and the normal nerve
conduction ﬁndings, the possibility that his syndrome had
been induced by a peripheral neuropathic process seems
very unlikely. Finally, the presence of painful spasms preci-
pitated by various stimuli, as well as the favourable response
to diazepam, that probably acts via central GABA-ergic
mechanisms, do not support the extrapyramidal nature of
his clinical picture.
It remains unknown whether our patient revealed anti-
GAD or anti-amphyphysin antibodies, since the correspond-
ing assay was not performed. The possible detection of these
antibodies would further support the diagnosis of SPS,
although in about 30 –40% of SPS cases the former are not
detectable. The manifestation of the neurological syndrome
in our patient a few days after initiation of isotretinoin treat-
ment and its rapid reversibility following cessation of ther-
apy strongly suggest that this drug was responsible for the
observed clinical and electrophysiological ﬁndings. More-
over, the absence of conditions known to be associated with
SPS or stiff-person like syndrome [4,6], i.e. autoimmune
disease, endocrinopathy, neoplasm, electrolytic disturbance
or additional neurological de ﬁcit, either prior to the
syndrome manifestation or during the 5-year follow-up,

provides further support to our hypothesis. Due to the sever-
ity of the syndrome we abstained from re-challenging the
patient with isotretinoin considering this trial as ethically
unacceptable.
It is well known that synthetic retinoids, like vitamin A,
are capable of affecting the development, differentiation and
function of nervous system [1,2]. Side effects involving the
central nervous system (CNS) that are deﬁnitely or probably
related to oral isotretinoin administration include headache,
depression and disul ﬁram-like reactions [2]. To the best of
our knowledge, our patient is theﬁrst case of SPS associated
with oral isotretinoin therapy. Interestingly, a mild stiff
person-like syndrome restricted to the legs has been
reported by the Ann Arbor group in a psoriatic patient
during oral therapy with another retinoid, etretinate [7]. In
a more recent paper of this group the follow-up of this case
and two further cases of muscle rigidity related to this
compound were published [8]. These cases reveal signi ﬁ-
cant differences, as compared to our patient. In contrast to
the latter, they are characterized by a relatively limited
muscle stiffness without: (a) painful superimposed spasms,
(b) precipitation by various stimuli, (c) concurrent activity
of antagonist muscle pairs on electromyography and (d)
favourable response to diazepam [8]. These cases taken
